solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Things won't change what vet users must!

indicators.note: must, read as the noun for new grape juice before fermenting, or as compulsion, signals the letters of the words before it are set to work in a new order

explanation.surface: An exclamation about the regime pet owners have to follow at the vet's surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must' looks like a verb ending the sentence but is the anagram signal for WHAT VET USERS, giving the twelve letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a resigned saying meaning it has always been so, so nothing will ever alter.

clue.text: Highlight of magic act not entirely affected?

indicators.note: not entirely means the phrase for the show's best moment loses its final letter

parts.note: the star turn of a conjuror's act could be called THE A TRICK, its top-grade trick

explanation.surface: Wonders whether the big moment of a conjuror's show was rather overdone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not entirely' cuts the last letter K from THE A TRICK.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatric means showy or exaggerated, as affected behaviour is put on for display.

clue.text: Grenade Quatermass secures all right

indicators.note: secures means the two names hold the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: A grenade attack is foiled by Professor Quatermass, the TV science-fiction hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Quatermass was a scientist hero of 1950s British TV and film science fiction.
explanation.definitionFit: Something adequate is acceptable, merely satisfactory, as 'all right' says.

clue.text: Will reductio ad absurdum reach this flannelled fool?

definitions.meaning: an argument that pushes a claim to an absurd conclusion
Kipling's phrase for a cricketer in white flannels

explanation.surface: Wonders whether a logical argument taken to absurdity could ever get through to a dim cricketer.
explanation.walkthrough: SILLY POINT is a cricket fielding position close in on the off side, a famously exposed spot; 'flannelled fools' comes from a 1903 Kipling poem mocking cricketers.
explanation.definitionFit: A reduction to absurdity ends at a ridiculous conclusion, and the close fielder in that cricket position is likewise named for it.

clue.text: Refashioning God and Christ? Insane!

indicators.note: refashioning means the three words that follow are remade, their letters put in a new order

explanation.surface: An outraged believer protests at someone remaking God and Christ to suit themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the instruction to rearrange GOD CHRIST INSANE and the scandalised cry it produces.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the stock outraged protest when something holy or revered is tampered with.

clue.text: Such editorialising characterised by "1 Down" and "anal"?

definitions.text: Such editorialising characterised by "1 Down" and "anal"?

parts.words: Such editorialising characterised by "1 Down" and "anal"
parts.note: editorials in a newspaper go by this name, and the two quoted words each start with articles: the and a, then an and a

explanation.surface: Mocks newspaper opinion pieces as showy and fussily obsessive.
explanation.walkthrough: 1 Down is THEATRIC, which opens THE A, while ANAL opens AN A: both lead with two articles.
explanation.definitionFit: Editorials expressing a newspaper's own opinion are called by this name in British usage.

clue.text: Where we may recreate Hamlet as Thelma?

definitions.text: Where we may recreate Hamlet as Thelma?

parts.words: Where we may recreate Hamlet as Thelma
parts.note: recreate means to play, so this is a place for recreation; also turning the name Hamlet into Thelma is a play (a drama) ground up, its letters jumbled

explanation.surface: Suggests a place where an amateur company might stage Shakespeare with a gender-swapped lead.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet and Thelma share the same letters, so the title of a play has been ground into a new order.
explanation.definitionFit: A playground is where children recreate, that is take part in play and recreation.

clue.text: A Van Gogh grows on one

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the word for grows sits below, after the numeral

parts.note: one is I in Roman numerals
grows means RISES, increases

explanation.surface: A Van Gogh painting is said to grow on a viewer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Irises' (1889) is one of Van Gogh's best-known paintings.
explanation.definitionFit: Irises is the title of a famous painting by Vincent van Gogh, so it is one example of his work.

clue.text: Locum Doctor? As per broadcast, he holds the title

indicators.note: as per broadcast means the actor's surname is meant as heard over the airwaves

parts.note: David Tennant played the Doctor in Doctor Who for a spell, a temporary Doctor like a locum

explanation.surface: A stand-in doctor is described as holding a title, as reported on the news.
explanation.walkthrough: Doctor Who is a British TV series whose lead is recast every few years; each actor is effectively a temporary Doctor.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenant holds land or property by legal title as an occupant, from Latin tenere, to hold.

clue.text: See 1
So idiot gets it off in the sun?

parts.note: the fool's word that the answer, read as an instruction, acts on: cleared of its inner letters, it leaves the pronoun the clue goes on to name

explanation.surface: Asks whether a fool finally understands the joke, or perhaps gets lucky, while lying in the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'So' and 'gets' are links. Read the answer as an instruction: put IDIOT on vacation, vacating (emptying) its middle, and it gets IT.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone away from work on holiday, perhaps sunbathing abroad, is described with this phrase.

clue.text: See 1
Occupying pod, this obsessed fan catches band live

indicators.note: catches means the word for a fan holds the following pieces inside it, as if trapping them

parts.note: a STAN is slang for an obsessive fan, from the Eminem song
a ring is a band, as on a finger
to live is to BE, exist

explanation.surface: A devoted fan, sitting in a pod, manages to see a band perform live.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is cryptic: the vegetable is the thing found inside a pod.
explanation.definitionFit: This long thin vegetable grows in a pod, so it is the thing occupying one.

clue.text: Fine compiler writes country club devious clue about some whisky?

parts.note: F is an abbreviation for fine, as on pencil leads

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the setter's phrase and the club
devious means the word clue takes an indirect, twisted route, its letters rearranged

parts.note: the compiler is I, the setter, and writes is DO, does it: I DO
the UN is a club of countries, a crossword convention

explanation.surface: A setter writes a twisty clue about a country club's whisky.
explanation.definitionFit: A fluid ounce is a measure of liquid, so a quantity of whisky might be poured in it; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Surely Io's most effective solver

parts.note: Io is the setter, so 'Io's' stands for 'I am', I'M
a telling blow is a highly effective one
the solver is addressed as YOU

explanation.surface: The setter claims, presumably with tongue in cheek, to be the most effective solver of all.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic assertion, as in 'certainly, believe me', which is what 'surely' can express.

clue.text: The top feature for sleazy tourist?

definitions.text: The top feature for sleazy tourist?

indicators.note: in a down clue the top is the opening letter, so the top of the word sleazy is taken

parts.note: a TRIPPER is a tourist on an outing

explanation.surface: Asks what the main attraction is for a seedy holidaymaker.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: a striptease act is the top attraction for a sleazy tourist.
explanation.definitionFit: A stripper is a performer who undresses, the obvious lure a sleazy visitor would seek out.

clue.text: Alcohol has blackener in it, IMO

indicators.note: has, with 'in it' later, means the spirit holds something
in it, with 'has', means the alcohol holds the blackening substance inside

parts.note: METHS is methylated spirit, a denatured alcohol
INK blackens paper

explanation.surface: An opinion that some alcoholic drink contains a dark colouring.
explanation.walkthrough: IMO is texting shorthand for 'in my opinion'.
explanation.definitionFit: Methinks is an archaic way of saying 'it seems to me', the same as the abbreviation for 'in my opinion'.

clue.text: Get rid of Anne's nasty root problem

indicators.note: nasty describes the phrase before it as messed up, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: the name Anne; the 's is read as 'is', linking fodder to indicator

explanation.surface: Someone wants to be rid of Anne, who is unpleasant, or of her nasty problem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nasty' signals rearranging GET RID OF ANNE. FINGER-AND-TOE is another name for clubroot, a disease that swells the roots of turnips and cabbages.
explanation.definitionFit: Clubroot is a plant disease of the roots, and finger-and-toe is a traditional name for it.

clue.text: A lead actor in The Ladykillers who's kept cool

indicators.note: who's kept means the actor is held inside the symbol for the metal

parts.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
Herbert Lom acted in the 1955 Ealing comedy The Ladykillers

explanation.surface: A leading man in the Ealing comedy who managed to stay calm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lead actor' reads as one phrase but splits in two: the metal, then the actor. The Ladykillers is a 1955 British comedy film.
explanation.definitionFit: Aplomb is self-assured composure, the quality of someone who stays cool under pressure.

clue.text: Verse form is right on key

parts.note: DEL is the delete key on a keyboard

explanation.surface: A statement that a poetic form is perfectly suited, right on the mark.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondel is a short poem with a fixed pattern of rhymes and refrains, a type of poem.

clue.text: Moving to the sun, dishonestly obtained rides in ferries and cabs?

indicators.note: rides in means the word for stolen travels inside the ferry company's name

parts.note: P&O is a British ferry company, written PO
HOT is slang for stolen
cabs are TAXIS

explanation.surface: Someone heads for the sunshine, riding on stolen tickets in ferries and taxis.
explanation.walkthrough: P&O is a well-known British ferry operator. PHOTOTAXIS is the movement of an organism towards light.
explanation.definitionFit: Phototaxis is the biological term for an organism moving in response to light, such as towards sunlight.

clue.text: Model whom painter's welcoming so heartily

indicators.note: model as a verb means to shape, so these letters are reshaped into a new order

explanation.surface: An artist's model whom the painter greets warmly into the studio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' looks like a noun, the sitter, but is the signal to rearrange WHOM PAINTER'S, apostrophe dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Greeting someone with arms spread to embrace them is an idiom for a warm, eager reception.

clue.text: As a rule what Serbian uses to pay International Airport guards

indicators.note: guards means the airport's name stands around the following pieces, protecting them

parts.note: Orly is an airport serving Paris
the dinar is the Serbian currency

explanation.surface: A puzzle about the money a Serb would pay security staff at an international airport.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something as a rule means doing it normally or usually, which this adverb conveys.

clue.text: See 21
What client is leaving barber — jumble!

parts.note: a customer leaving a barber after a haircut is BALDER than before
the punctuation mark in the clue is a DASH

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses as rubbish the state a customer is in leaving the barber's.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed dash is not punctuation but a piece of the wordplay, naming itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Balderdash is nonsense, senseless talk, which a jumble of words amounts to.
